Social media skyrocketed in popularity since its inception in the early 2000s. After the rise and fall of basic social media sites like Six Degrees, Myspace hit the scene in 2003. By 2006, Myspace was the most visited website on the planet. By 2008, Facebook had overshadowed Myspace and became the “new” social media platform. Twitter, Reddit, Instagram, and Snapchat were all launched by 2011, and TikTok, the short-form video-sharing site, started in 2016. Today, more than 5 billion out of 7.88 billion people use mobile devices like cell phones. Visiting social media platforms is one of the main functions of these devices. One of the initial goals of social media sites was to help people connect with family, friends, and people they may have never met in person digitally, but they have become much more than that. Social media is now a space for political debate, advertising, and cultural taste-making.

Social media has changed how people interact and live their lives for better and  worse. Teens and young adults are the groups that use social media the most. Like most forms of technology, social media has both pros and cons. Social media can be a great platform for learning, connecting, and entertainment. In a recent study, about half of the 1,500 teens surveyed said social media is important for them to get support, feel less alone, and express themselves. They also said that social media helped them to feel less depressed and anxious. However, studies show that social media is strongly linked to anxiety and depression in teens. Mental health outcomes are worse for those who use social media very frequently. Also, the more severe teens’ symptoms were, the more anxious, lonely, and depressed they felt after using social media.

Neuroscientists at the University of North Carolina used brain scans to study the effects of social media on pre-teen and teen brains. They studied middle schoolers between the ages of 12 and 15 over several years. They found that middle schoolers who checked social media a lot compared to those who did not were much more sensitive to social rewards. It is too soon to tell if this fact is helpful, harmful, or neutral. Social sensitivity could be a good thing, showing that the teens are learning to connect with others. It could also lead to social anxiety and depression if social needs are unmet. What is clear is that social media has an impact on the reward pathways in our brains. Researchers have also found that social media use can shorten attention spans. This makes it harder to focus on things that don’t bring instant enjoyment.

Teens and young adults who use social media frequently are three times more likely to suffer from depression. Suicide rates among females aged 15-24 have increased by 87 percent over the last 20 years and 30 percent in males in the same range. These statistics could result from many factors, but self-reports and research indicate that social media plays a role for many. Smartphones and social media platforms are designed to be addictive. We feel happy when we reach for our phones or see notifications. However, the content we engage with is often manipulated and can have negative effects. One example of this is edited photos that present unattainable beauty standards. These images impact self-esteem for many, especially young women. One in three teen girls reports that social media worsens their body image issues. The online world can change the way we see ourselves in the real world.
